articles.title: Leonids All Over
articles.summary: This article compiles multiple firsthand accounts of observations during the Leonids meteor shower. Observers from various locations reported seeing numerous bright meteors, with some exceptionally brilliant (brighter than Sirius, brighter than Jupiter, or even -6 magnitude) despite varying sky conditions, including partial cloud cover and light pollution. Many of these dazzling meteors left visible trails lasting several seconds.

articles.title: SJAA Activities Calendar
articles.summary: The SJAA Activities Calendar outlines the San Jose Astronomical Association's events for January and February, including multiple star parties at Houge Park and Fremont Peak with details on sunset and moon phases. It also lists observational astronomy classes and general meetings featuring talks on deep-sky observing and member presentations on various observing plans. The calendar provides contact information and a note about insurance coverage for members.

articles.title: Editor's Extras David North
articles.summary: David North is stepping down as editor of the Ephemeris after two years, with Jane Houston and Morris (Mojo) Jones taking over. North will remain involved, continuing his "Mooning" column, condensing meteor notes, and handling publishing tasks like printing and mailing list generation. He reflects on his time as editor as an amazing experience.

articles.title: Get Your 1999 SJAA "Astronomical Pocket Diary"
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) is promoting its 1999 "Astronomical Pocket Diary," a custom appointment calendar and astronomical almanac available to members for $10. This announcement is featured in the January 1999 official publication of the SJAA, with more details found on page 6.

articles.title: From Page One
articles.summary: This document compiles several individual observing reports from various locations across California and Arizona, detailing meteor sightings. Observers describe varying numbers of meteors, their brightness, and the duration of their trails, with many noting fast and bright events, including Leonids. Despite some challenging weather conditions, observers generally reported good shows, with one observer even developing unique nomenclature for different types of meteors.

articles.title: Leonids at Fremont Peak-- All Two Of Them (or "The Wrong Shower")
articles.summary: The author attempted to observe the Leonid meteor shower at Fremont Peak on November 16, but encountered extremely poor weather conditions including heavy fog, drizzle, rain, and strong winds throughout the night. Despite high hopes for clearer skies, only two meteors were briefly sighted during a short break in the fog. The observation session was largely a disappointment due to persistent clouds and precipitation.

articles.title: Leonids From Henry Coe Park:
articles.summary: Despite initial overcast weather, the author, Jack Zeiders, embarked on an impromptu trip to observe the Leonids meteor shower near Henry Coe Park. He successfully viewed numerous bright meteors from various roadside locations, including sighting several fireballs and two 10-minute counts of 6 and 7 Leonids respectively, though a photography attempt was thwarted by camera trouble. He also encountered fellow observer Jim Van Nuland, who had given up due to the weather at a higher elevation.

articles.title: Bob Garfinkle
articles.summary: The author recounts his experience observing the Leonids meteor shower from a convertible in southeastern Georgia on November 16-17, 1998. Despite initial low rates and challenging conditions like atmospheric haze and later fog, he observed an increase in meteor activity before viewing was curtailed by heavy mist and dropping temperatures. The article also includes an editor's note about the author, Bob Garfinkle, being elected a Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society.

articles.title: Jane Houston
articles.summary: A group of amateur astronomers, including Jane Houston, ventured to Mercey Hot Springs on November 16th to observe the Leonid Meteor Storm. Despite initial dismal weather, heavy clouds, and rain that made observations difficult, the persistent group eventually witnessed a thrilling display of bright meteors, fireballs, and the Zodiacal Light during a clearing later in the night. The report details the challenges and the eventual success of the meteor watch.

articles.title: Jay Freeman
articles.summary: Jay Freeman recounts attending a captivating public lecture by physicist Steven W. Hawking in San Jose, where Hawking discussed a wide array of topics including the future of humanity through genetic engineering, the development of artificial intelligence, advancements in physics like unified field theory, and cosmic phenomena. The article also highlights Hawking's unique communication method via speech synthesis and his inspiring interaction with disabled youth, emphasizing his profound impact beyond pure science.

articles.title: The Many Faces Of Dr. Jay
articles.summary: The article introduces "Dr. Jay" through his various humorous personas and professional titles. It then transitions to a detailed technical discussion on measuring optical fabrication errors, explaining how different testing parameters—such as peak-to-valley versus RMS, wavefront versus mirror, and light wavelength—can lead to significantly varied "wave" ratings for the same mirror. The author stresses the importance of understanding these testing details to accurately interpret optical quality.

articles.title: Activities Through Other Clubs
articles.summary: This article outlines astronomical activities offered by other clubs, encouraging San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) members to participate. The Telescope Makers Workshop (TAC) provides access to the Montebello site on Wednesdays for observing, while the Peninsula Astronomical Society (PAS) hosts public night viewing at Foothill Observatory on Friday evenings and solar viewing on Saturday mornings. PAS also has a general meeting on 'Little Black Holes' and a board meeting scheduled for January.

articles.title: Akkana Peck
articles.summary: This document provides an observing guide for January, detailing the visibility of various planets. It notes Mercury's increasing difficulty, Venus's prominence in the evening, and Mars's growth towards opposition. Highlights include Jupiter's excellent detail with two double shadow transits, Saturn's observability and ring shadow, and a lunar occultation of Aldebaran on January 26.

articles.title: Astronomical Pocket Diary
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) is offering a custom 1999 "Astronomical Pocket Diary" for $10, functioning as both an appointment calendar and an astronomical almanac. It features daily rise/set times, lunar phases, meteor showers, and SJAA-specific event dates. All profits from the sales are tax-deductible donations that support the club's Equipment Loaner Program.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article details a highly favorable lunar observing period, focusing on an Aldebaran occultation on the 26th and numerous other occultations within the Hyades. It highlights several lunar features for observation, including prominent craters like Copernicus and Clavius, and various rilles and formations across the lunar surface, emphasizing ideal lighting conditions over multiple nights.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article discusses the Quadrantids meteor shower, which peaks around January 2nd and is associated with comet 96P/Macholz. Despite its potential for over 100 meteors per hour during its brief, intense maximum, the 1999 display was expected to be significantly reduced to 10-20 meteors per hour due to interference from a full moon. Observers were advised to begin observations at midnight, with the shower best seen around 5 am local time.

articles.title: Mainly Europa
articles.summary: Dr. Jeff Moore of the NASA AMES Research Center gave a talk on Europa, presenting incredible images from the Galileo mission. He focused on evidence for plate tectonics and a liquid sub-ice ocean on Europa, supported by observations of crust extension, 'bunny head' ice ponds, and flooded craters. The discussion also briefly touched upon Ganymede and Callisto.

articles.title: Editor's Extras
articles.summary: This 'Editor's Extras' serves as a farewell from an outgoing editor, reflecting on the club's recent stabilization, the rebuilding of the Fremont Peak observatory, and the transition to new leadership. It deeply mourns the passing of member Alan Nelms, celebrating his gentle character and enthusiasm rather than just his observational skills. The article also announces a new astronomy class instructor and reports recent wind damage to the Fremont Peak Observatory roof.

articles.title: December Board Notes
articles.summary: The December 4th board meeting covered various club affairs, including the approval of the calendar and past minutes, and the payment of AANC dues. Discussions also addressed improving clarity for 'no host' Fremont Peak events to manage visitor expectations. Additionally, the board approved funding for Ephemeris mailing, announced six candidates for the upcoming board elections, and urgently sought a replacement for the outgoing Treasurer, Bob Elsberry.

articles.title: Candidates For Next Year
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) nominating committee (Mark Taylor, Terry Kahl, Bill Arnett) has announced an initial list of candidates for the upcoming board of directors election, including David North, Akkana Peck, Jim Bartolini, Jim Van Nuland, Morris Jones, and Bill O'Shaughnessy. The article details eligibility requirements for candidates (one year of membership or six board meetings attended) and lists the specific seats up for election, including one being vacated by resignation. The election is scheduled to take place during the February meeting, with nominations also accepted from the floor.

articles.title: Celestial Calendar
articles.summary: This Celestial Calendar, compiled by Richard Stanton, provides detailed astronomical data for January 1999, tailored for observers in the PDT timezone. It features lunar phases, rise, transit, and set times for the Moon and five major planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn), alongside their magnitudes, distances, right ascension, and declination. Additionally, it offers information on hours of darkness, twilight periods, sidereal time, and identifies an optimal 'Darkest Saturday Night' for observing.

articles.title: Don Machholz
articles.summary: This article, attributed to Don Machholz, provides an update on current comet visibility and recent discoveries, detailing several comets observable in the sky and their orbital characteristics. It highlights newly found comets from November 1998 (Spahr, Hergenrother, LINEAR), the reclassification of C/1939 TN (Vaisala-Oterma) as a comet, and includes a note on the passing of comet discoverer Father Leo Boehtin.

articles.title: Ephemerides -- Epoch 2000, 0h UTC
articles.summary: This document provides detailed ephemerides for several comets, including 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, C/1998 U3 (Jager), C/1998 P1 (Williams), C/1998 M5 (Linear), 52P/Harrington-Abell, and C/1998 U5 (Linear). The data, set for Epoch 2000, 0h UTC, spans from January 2 to February 6 and includes Right Ascension, Declination, Elongation, Sky position, and Visual Magnitude. This information is crucial for astronomers and observers to locate and track these celestial objects.

articles.title: Orbital Elements -- Epoch 2000.0
articles.summary: This document presents a table of orbital elements for six celestial objects, including comets such as Giacobini-Zinner, Jager, and LINEAR, all referenced to Epoch 2000.0. For each object, parameters like perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, orbital period, absolute magnitude, and data source are provided. This data appears to be part of an ephemeris from January 1999.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and members of the Board of Directors for an organization. It details the names, respective roles such as President, VP, Secretary, Treasurer, and Directors, along with their associated contact phone numbers. This serves as a directory for the organization's leadership.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document lists the staff and contact information for the "Ephemeris" publication and its associated programs. It details key personnel responsible for editorial, circulation, and printing, alongside leaders for community astronomy initiatives such as a mentoring program, observational astronomy education, school star parties, and a telescope loaner program. Contact phone numbers and an email address are provided for each role or service.

articles.title: Submit
articles.summary: This document encourages members to submit articles for publication in the SJAA Ephemeris. Submissions should be sent via email to Dave North at Timocharis@aol.com.

articles.title: Astro Ads
articles.summary: This document features an advertisement for a used Meade 8" LX3 Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope with accessories, priced at $750 obo. Additionally, it provides an important notice about SJAA Star Parties, clarifying that they are "no host" events without official greeters or guaranteed attendance in inclement weather, serving as recommended viewing locations for enthusiasts.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Program Status
articles.summary: This article provides an update on the Telescope Loaner Program, indicating its current status and availability to all SJAA members. Interested members can contact Mike Koop at the provided phone number to utilize the program.

articles.title: Current Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists telescopes currently loaned out to various individuals, along with their respective due dates. It informs interested parties that they can be placed on a waiting list for a scope once it becomes available after its return date.

articles.title: Extended Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists astronomical telescopes that have had their loan periods extended, indicating they are still with their current borrowers. It outlines a process for interested individuals to borrow one of these scopes by arranging a transfer time with the existing borrower. The list includes various telescope types, borrower names, and original due dates.

articles.title: Available Scopes
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) provides a list of telescopes immediately available for loan to its members. These scopes, which include various Newtonian, Dobsonian, and Refractor types, are stored at different member homes, and interested individuals should contact Mike Koop to arrange pickup at SJAA events.

articles.title: Waiting List
articles.summary: This brief article, titled "Waiting List," notes a "Solar Scope" for Dave North and asks readers for help with storing one or two astronomical scopes. Individuals with available storage space are encouraged to contact Mike Koop via phone or email to assist with this need.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The SJAA Ephemeris, the official newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published monthly throughout the year, from January to December, totaling 12 issues annually. The publication is associated with the San Jose Astronomical Association, located at 5380 Pebbletree Way.

articles.title: To Subscribe to/Unsubscribe from the SJAA Mailing List send email to
articles.summary: This document provides instructions on how to subscribe to or unsubscribe from the SJAA (San Jose Astronomical Association) mailing list. Users need to send an email to sjaa-request@seds.org with a blank subject line and a single text line containing either "subscribe" or "unsubscribe". This information was published in the January 1999 edition of the SJAA EPHEMERIS.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing membership options for adults ($15) and juniors ($6), with an additional cost for a Sky & Telescope subscription. It provides instructions for submitting the form and payment via check to the treasurer by mail or at an SJAA meeting, along with contact information for the organization.
